# APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation

Sirui Zhang ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work done during internship in MSRA.

###### Abstract

Post-training is crucial for improving text-to-image models, yet
existing pipelines typically rely on manually curated training data and
fixed training distributions. We introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training),
a fully automated framework that adaptively post-trains a base model
according to its evolving capability profile. APT coordinates three
agents to construct evaluation sets from user requirements, diagnose
model-specific strengths and failure modes, and generate reinforcement
learning data with an adaptive prompt distribution that emphasizes
underperforming capabilities. By repeatedly evaluating, diagnosing, and
updating the generator, APT lets the current model’s behavior shape its
next training tasks, forming a feedback loop inspired by recursive
self-improvement. For general-purpose settings without user-specified
evaluation scenarios, we further develop an evaluation harness that
enables broad and diverse evaluation set generation. Experiments across
multiple base models, benchmarks, and generation architectures
demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic,
architecture-agnostic, and fully automated.

the Diagnosis Agent evaluates the current model on these pairs to
identify its strengths and failure modes; and the RL Data Generation
Agent adaptively samples next-round training prompts, prioritizing
underperforming capabilities. The updated model is then re-evaluated in
the next round, allowing the training distribution to continuously adapt
to the model’s evolving capability profile. This design eliminates the
need for manually curated post-training data and makes APT
model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, architecture-agnostic, and fully
automated.

## 1 Introduction

Recent text-to-image (T2I) models have achieved remarkable progress in
visual quality, prompt following, text rendering, compositional
generation, and controllability ([Black Forest Labs, 2025](#bib.bib14);
[OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib12); [Google, 2026](#bib.bib16); [SeedDance,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)). Beyond large-scale
pre-training, post-training has become increasingly important for
correcting specific failure modes and aligning model behavior with
desired objectives ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6); [Jiang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib21); [Feng et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib17)). Existing post-training pipelines, however,
typically rely on manually constructed training distributions:
practitioners identify model weaknesses, collect or synthesize
corresponding training data, and repeatedly adjust the data distribution
based on empirical observations ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Chen et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib6); [Feng et al., 2026b](#bib.bib17); [Geng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18)). Such a workflow is labor-intensive and difficult to
scale as models, benchmarks, and user requirements continue to
diversify.

More fundamentally, we argue that post-training should be
_model-adaptive_. Different base models exhibit substantially different
capability distributions: a model that performs well on text rendering
may struggle with counting or spatial relations, while another may
exhibit the opposite behavior. Consequently, a post-training dataset
that is effective for one model is not necessarily optimal for another.
We can view each base model $`M`$ as inducing its own capability and
failure distribution $`p_{M}`$ over generation tasks. Effective
post-training should therefore identify where the current model
underperforms, sample training examples accordingly ([Chen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib26)), and continuously adapt the sampling distribution as
the model improves ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)). In other words, the
key question is not only _how to optimize a model_, but also _what the
current model should be trained on_. This perspective naturally connects
post-training to recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the
evaluation results of the updated model are used to determine the
training tasks for the next round ([Zelikman et al., 2023](#bib.bib27);
[Zweiger et al., 2026](#bib.bib28); [Huang et al., 2026](#bib.bib29)).

To address this problem, we introduce APT (Agentic Post-Training), a
fully automated framework that turns post-training into an adaptive,
evaluation-driven self-improvement loop, as illustrated in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
Given a T2I base model and an evaluation requirement, APT automatically
constructs an evaluation set of prompt–rubric pairs, diagnoses the
current model’s strengths and weaknesses, and generates model-specific
RL training data. The updated model is then re-evaluated, allowing its
evolving behavior to continuously reshape the training distribution for
the next round. Rather than relying on a fixed, manually curated
dataset, APT lets the current model determine what should be learned
next.

As shown in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
APT is built around three collaborative agents. The Evaluation Set
Generation Agent converts a high-level evaluation scope into a
structured evaluation suite with an adaptive taxonomy, prompts, and
task-specific rubrics. The Diagnosis Agent evaluates the current model
at the instance and category levels and summarizes systematic strengths
and failure modes. The RL Data Generation Agent then converts this
diagnosis into an adaptive prompt distribution that prioritizes
underperforming capabilities while retaining moderate and mastered ones,
producing model-specific data for RL-based post-training ([Zheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22); [Liu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib23); [Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24)). Repeated evaluation, diagnosis, and adaptive
sampling provide an implicit mechanism for discovering and tracking the
evolving model-dependent distribution $`p_{M}`$ without explicitly
estimating it.

APT also supports general-purpose post-training when no evaluation scope
is specified. For this setting, we develop an evaluation harness that
guides the Evaluation Set Generation Agent to systematically construct a
broad and diverse evaluation set spanning common generation scenarios
and capability dimensions ([Feng et al., 2026c](#bib.bib25)).

The resulting framework is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic,
architecture-agnostic, and fully automated, and we validate these
properties across multiple T2I models, generation architectures, and
benchmarks ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib6); [Esser et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7); [Black Forest Labs, 2024](#bib.bib8); [Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). APT consistently
improves diverse base models and outperforms post-training with a
carefully handcrafted RL training set. Moreover, transferring
APT-generated training data across models is consistently inferior to
adaptively generating data for the target model, supporting our central
hypothesis that effective post-training distributions are model-specific
and should evolve together with the model. Together, these results
establish agentic, evaluation-driven adaptation as a practical step
toward recursive self-improvement for text-to-image generation.

## 2 Method

Overview.
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation")
provides an overview of APT. The Evaluation Set Generation Agent is
invoked once before post-training to construct the fixed evaluation set
$`\mathcal{E}`$ of prompt–rubric pairs
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Evaluation Set Generation Agent ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation")).
Users may specify an evaluation scope; when no scope is provided, we use
our general-purpose evaluation harness to ensure broad and comprehensive
coverage. APT then enters an iterative post-training loop. At each
round, the Diagnosis Agent
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Diagnosis Agent ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"))
evaluates the current model and produces an evaluation report, which is
passed to the RL Data Generation Agent
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 RL Data Generation Agent ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"))
to generate training data for the next RL update. This RSI-inspired loop
repeats after each update, enabling the training distribution to adapt
to the model’s evolving weaknesses. As described in
Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 General, Adaptive, and Fully Automated Post-Training ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
APT is model-agnostic, benchmark-agnostic, and architecture-agnostic,
and can therefore be applied to diverse text-to-image models and
evaluation settings.

Round-Wise Learning Objective. At the beginning of round $`t`$,
$`M_{t}`$ denotes the current text-to-image generator; $`p`$ and $`x`$
denote a text prompt and a generated image, respectively. Let $`D_{t}`$
be the generated dataset of training prompts for this round, and write
$`(p,R)\sim D_{t}`$ to denote sampling a prompt–rubric-set pair from
this dataset. For a prompt $`p_{i}`$, let $`R_{i}`$ be its associated
rubric set and $`\rho\in R_{i}`$ an individual evaluation criterion.
Both diagnosis and training use GPT-4.1-mini as vision-language
evaluator, denoted by $`V`$. Its binary output $`V(x,p,\rho)\in\{0,1\}`$
is $`1`$ if image $`x`$ satisfies criterion $`\rho`$ for prompt $`p`$,
and $`0`$ otherwise. For an image $`x_{i}`$ generated from $`p_{i}`$,
the training reward is the arithmetic mean of these rubric-level scores:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
r(x_{i},p_{i})=\frac{1}{|R_{i}|}\sum_{\rho\in R_{i}}V(x_{i},p_{i},\rho).
``` |  |

Each prompt’s rubric set is fixed and shared across all its generated
images within a rollout round. The evaluator’s scoring instructions are
provided in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Prompt for RL Reward Generation ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
The round-wise expected-reward objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(M_{t})=\mathbb{E}_{(p,R)\sim D_{t},\,x\sim M_{t}(\cdot\mid p)}\!\left[r(x,p)\right].
``` |  | (1) |

Starting from $`M_{t}`$, the configured RL algorithm takes a finite
number of optimization steps aimed at increasing $`J(M_{t})`$, with
$`D_{t}`$ and the reward procedure fixed within the round.

Recursive Data–Model Coupling. APT couples an *outer loop of
diagnostic-driven task adaptation* with an *inner loop of RL-based model
optimization*. At round $`t`$, $`\mathcal{B}_{t}\subset\mathcal{E}`$ is
a sampled diagnostic batch of prompt–rubric pairs, and
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$ denotes the resulting rubric-level evaluation report
for $`M_{t}`$. Let $`\operatorname{Diag}`$ and $`\mathcal{G}`$ denote
the diagnosis and data-generation procedures, respectively, and let
$`\mathcal{U}`$ denote the RL update operator. The coupled update is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\operatorname{Diag}(M_{t},\mathcal{B}_{t}),\qquad D_{t}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{R}_{t}),`$ |  | (2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle M_{t+1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}(M_{t},D_{t};V).`$ |  |  |

The update operator $`\mathcal{U}`$ returns $`M_{t+1}`$ by applying the
configured finite number of RL steps to $`M_{t}`$, with the aim of
maximizing $`J(M_{t})`$ in
Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
Re-evaluating $`M_{t+1}`$ yields a diagnostic report
$`\mathcal{R}_{t+1}`$ that guides the generation of training prompts
$`D_{t+1}`$ for the next RL update. We next describe the three agents
that instantiate this feedback-driven post-training loop.

![Refer to caption](2610.18097v1/agent-1-v2.png)

Figure 2: Left: Statistics of the sub-categories within each category
and the prompt-rubrics pairs within each category. All prompt-rubrics

### 2.1 Evaluation Set Generation Agent

The Evaluation Set Generation Agent is responsible for constructing the
evaluation data used to diagnose the current model before the
post-training stage. When a user specifies an evaluation scope, the
agent directly generates evaluation examples tailored to the requested
scenarios. For the more general setting where no evaluation scope is
provided, we further design a general-purpose evaluation harness that
guides the agent to systematically construct a broad-coverage evaluation
set spanning diverse image-generation scenarios and capabilities. Each
evaluation example consists of an image-generation prompt paired with
its corresponding prompt-specific evaluation rubrics. The evaluation set
is constructed through a multi-step generation pipeline consisting of
scenario generation, prompt generation, and rubric generation.

Step 1: Scenario Generation. We begin with a broad set of common
image-generation scenario categories, including Human, Object, Animal,
Plant, Scene, Food, Event, Fictional World, Text, and UI and Graphic
Design. For each category, we prompt an LLM to generate dozens of
fine-grained sub-categories and corresponding items. For example, the
Human category may include sub-categories such as Race, Occupation, and
Gender, while the Occupation sub-category may further contain items such
as Researcher and Doctor. This process produces a hierarchical scenario
taxonomy that provides broad and structured coverage of diverse
image-generation scenarios.

Step 2: Prompt Generation. Given the items derived from the scenario
taxonomy, we further enrich them with a set of descriptive dimensions to
generate diverse image-generation prompts. These descriptions capture
common compositional and semantic requirements, such as attributes,
spatial relationships, object counts, interactions, and colors. For each
item, we randomly sample one to four descriptions and prompt GPT-4.1,
together with a predefined system prompt described in
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Prompt for Evaluation Prompt Generation ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
to synthesize the final image-generation prompt. For example, an item
such as Doctor can be combined with descriptions of color, interaction,
and spatial relationship to produce a more compositional and challenging
prompt. This design increases both the diversity and coverage of the
generated evaluation prompts.

Step 3: Rubric Generation. For each generated prompt, we further
construct prompt-specific evaluation rubrics ([Feng et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib25)). Concretely, we feed the prompt, together with the
rubric-generation system prompt described in
Appendix [E.2](#A5.SS2 "E.2 Prompt for Rubric Generation ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
into GPT-4.1-mini to generate up to 10 prompt-specific rubrics. These
rubrics specify the aspects that should be checked for the given prompt,
such as identity consistency, text correctness, style alignment, scene
correctness, spatial relations, or counting accuracy, depending on the
prompt content. As a result, each evaluation example is represented as a
prompt paired with its corresponding rubrics, enabling fine-grained and
task-aware diagnosis of model behavior.

Overall, the Evaluation Set Generation Agent transforms a high-level
evaluation requirement into a diverse evaluation set containing 2,609
prompt–rubrics pairs. Detailed statistics are provided in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
This evaluation set serves as the foundation for the subsequent
Diagnosis Agent, which analyzes model performance and drives the
adaptive post-training loop.

### 2.2 Diagnosis Agent

The Diagnosis Agent analyzes the performance of the current model on the
evaluation set and summarizes its strengths and weaknesses into a
structured evaluation report. At each post-training round $`t`$, we
randomly sample a batch
$`\mathcal{B}_{t}=\{(p_{i},R_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}\subset\mathcal{E}`$ of
prompt–rubric pairs, where $`N`$ is the diagnostic batch size ($`120`$
by default). The diagnosis process consists of two stages:
instance-level analysis and evaluation report construction.

Instance-Level Analysis. Within round $`t`$, let $`K_{i}=|R_{i}|`$ be
the number of rubrics for the $`i`$-th sampled prompt $`p_{i}`$, and let
$`\rho_{ij}`$ denote its $`j`$-th rubric. We generate an image
$`x_{i}^{(t)}`$ with the current model $`M_{t}`$ and use the same
evaluator $`V`$ as in the training reward to obtain the rubric score
$`s_{ij}^{(t)}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
x_{i}^{(t)}\sim M_{t}(\cdot\mid p_{i}),\qquad s_{ij}^{(t)}=V(x_{i}^{(t)},p_{i},\rho_{ij})\in\{0,1\}.
``` |  | (3) |

This yields a set of prompt-specific rubric-level evaluation results
$`E_{i}^{(t)}=\{(\rho_{ij},s_{ij}^{(t)})\}_{j=1}^{K_{i}}`$, providing a
fine-grained diagnosis of the current model for prompt $`p_{i}`$.

Evaluation Report Construction. After processing all $`N`$ sampled
prompt–rubric pairs, the Diagnosis Agent constructs the report
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}=\{(p_{i},E_{i}^{(t)})\}_{i=1}^{N}`$, instantiating the
diagnosis procedure $`\operatorname{Diag}`$ in
Equation [2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
Each entry in $`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$ contains the original prompt together
with its rubric-level evaluation results, where each result consists of
an evaluation rubric and its corresponding binary score. The resulting
report captures the current model’s successes and failures across
diverse generation capabilities and is subsequently passed to the RL
Data Generation Agent to guide the construction of training data for the
subsequent RL update.

### 2.3 RL Data Generation Agent

The RL Data Generation Agent takes the evaluation report produced by the
Diagnosis Agent as input and generates training prompts for the
subsequent RL update. Its main role is to identify recurring failure
patterns in the report, summarize the capabilities that should be
improved, and translate these findings into a model-specific training
distribution.

We use the evaluation report as an empirical characterization of the
current model’s capability distribution. This is feasible for several
reasons. First, the evaluation set is designed to provide broad coverage
over diverse generation scenarios and capabilities. As a result, the
sampled evaluation examples probe many different regions of the model’s
capability space rather than concentrating on a narrow
benchmark-specific domain. Second, each prompt is associated with
multiple prompt-specific rubrics, which provide fine-grained feedback on
*what* the model succeeds or fails on. Therefore, the report contains
not only whether a generation is successful, but also structured
evidence about the underlying capability responsible for the success or
failure. Third, modern language models such as GPT-5.4 have strong
summarization and reasoning capabilities, allowing them to compare
observations across many evaluation examples and identify recurring
patterns that may not be obvious from any individual sample. For
instance, prompts from different semantic categories may repeatedly fail
for the same underlying reason, such as accurate counting, rendering
text on objects, or preserving specific attributes. By aggregating these
cross-example patterns, the agent can infer which capabilities are
consistently underperforming and which are already handled reliably.
Finally, because the evaluation report is regenerated from the current
model at every post-training round, the inferred capability profile
naturally changes as the model improves. In this sense, the Diagnosis
Agent and RL Data Generation Agent together provide an implicit and
continually updated estimate of the model’s current performance
distribution, without requiring an additional explicitly trained
estimator.

Based on the summarized failure patterns, the RL Data Generation Agent
generates $`N_{\text{train}}`$ new prompts for the current round’s RL
update, with $`p_{t,k}^{\mathrm{train}}`$ denoting the $`k`$-th
generated prompt and $`R_{t,k}^{\mathrm{train}}`$ denoting its
corresponding rubric set generated by GPT-4.1-mini using the same
procedure and system prompt as for the evaluation set :

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
D_{t}=\mathcal{G}(\mathcal{R}_{t})=\{(p_{t,k}^{\mathrm{train}},R_{t,k}^{\mathrm{train}})\}_{k=1}^{N_{\text{train}}}.
``` |  | (4) |

This instantiates the data-generation procedure $`\mathcal{G}`$ in
Equation [2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
conditioned on the current model’s diagnostic report
$`\mathcal{R}_{t}`$. A clear majority of these prompts target recurring
weak capabilities, while a smaller portion covers moderately performing
and already-strong capabilities to preserve diversity and avoid
over-concentrating on a single failure mode. Since different base models
exhibit different patterns in the same broad evaluation space, this
process naturally produces model-specific training data. Moreover, as
the model evolves over successive rounds, the generated training
distribution is updated accordingly.

We implement the RL Data Generation Agent with GPT-5.4. The detailed
instruction prompt used by the agent is provided in
Appendix [E.4](#A5.SS4 "E.4 Prompt for the RL Data Generation Agent ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").

### 2.4 General, Adaptive, and Fully Automated Post-Training

APT is designed as a general post-training framework that can be applied
across different evaluation settings, base models, and generation
architectures without task-specific or model-specific redesign.
Specifically, APT is (1) benchmark-agnostic: it does not require
independently designed prompt sets for individual benchmarks, and a
single APT run can be evaluated across multiple T2I benchmarks; (2)
model-agnostic: the same agentic workflow can be directly applied to
diverse base models, including Lens ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib6)),
SD3.5 ([Esser et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)), FLUX ([Black Forest Labs,
2024](#bib.bib8)), and LongCat-Image ([Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib9));
(3) architecture-agnostic: APT is not tied to a particular
image-generation formulation and is effective for both diffusion-based
and autoregressive image-generation models ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Sun et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)); and (4) fully
automated: the evaluation results of the current model directly drive
the generation of prompts for subsequent RL updates, eliminating the
need for manually inspecting failures, designing training distributions,
or curating model-specific post-training data ([Xu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Geng et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)).

Recursive Self-Improvement for Text-to-Image Generation. APT brings
recursive self-improvement (RSI) ([Zelikman et al., 2023](#bib.bib27);
[Zweiger et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)) to text-to-image generation by
making the generator’s evolving capabilities drive the construction of
its own training curriculum. As formalized in
Equation [2](#S2.E2 "In 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
the current model produces behavioral evidence that agents translate
into targeted training tasks; RL updates the generator on these tasks,
and the updated generator provides fresh evidence for the next round.
This creates a recursive coupling between model optimization and task
construction: learning changes the model’s capability profile, which in
turn changes what the system trains on next. Through this feedback loop,
APT continually revises its training priorities in response to the
generator’s remaining and newly exposed weaknesses. By automating
diagnosis, curriculum construction, and RL updates, APT turns the
generator’s own successes and failures into actionable signals for
directing subsequent improvement. APT thus operationalizes RSI for T2I
post-training through an adaptive curriculum that evolves alongside the
model, replacing manual intervention in deciding what the model should
learn next.

Base T2I Models. To demonstrate that APT is model-agnostic, we apply it
to four diffusion-based T2I models: Lens ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6)), SD3.5-Medium ([Esser et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)),
FLUX.1 \[dev\] ([Black Forest Labs, 2024](#bib.bib8)), and
LongCat-Image ([Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)). We further evaluate
whether APT generalizes across model architectures by applying it to the
autoregressive image generator Janus-Pro ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)). We use the same APT agentic workflow across all
models, without introducing any model-specific prompt sets, reward
designs, or hyperparameter searches.

Benchmarks and Metrics. We evaluate on five widely used text-to-image
benchmarks that jointly cover compositional generation, prompt
following, and text rendering: GenEval ([Ghosh et al.,
2023](#bib.bib1)), GenEval2 ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)),
OneIG-EN ([Chang et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), DPG ([Hu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib4)), and CVTG-2K ([Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)). Details
of each benchmark are provided in
Section [C](#A3 "Appendix C Detailed Benchmark Results ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
Since the benchmark scores are reported on different scales, we
additionally report a normalized average by rescaling GenEval, OneIG-EN,
and CVTG-2K to the $`[0,100]`$ range and then averaging the scores
across all five benchmarks. Crucially, none of these benchmarks is used
to construct the training prompts: a single APT run produces one
post-trained model, which is then evaluated on all five benchmarks,
directly testing the benchmark-agnostic nature of APT described in
Section [2.4](#S2.SS4 "2.4 General, Adaptive, and Fully Automated Post-Training ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").

Implementation Details. We use DiffusionNFT ([Zheng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib22)) as our default RL algorithm for post-training. All
models are post-trained with LoRA (rank $`64`$, $`\alpha=128`$), using a
learning rate of $`3\mathrm{e}\text{-}4`$. During rollout, Lens,
SD3.5-M, and LongCat-Image use $`10`$ sampling steps, while FLUX.1
\[dev\] uses $`6`$ steps. The training resolution is $`768\times 768`$
for Lens and SD3.5-M, and $`512\times 512`$ for FLUX.1 \[dev\] and
LongCat-Image. For APT, each training round consists of $`20`$
optimization steps. At the beginning of each round, the Diagnosis Agent
samples $`120`$ prompt-rubrics pairs from the evaluation set generated
by the Evaluation Set Generation Agent and produces an evaluation
report. This report is then fed into the RL Data Generation Agent, which
automatically generates $`480`$ RL training prompts for the subsequent
training round. For the handcrafted RL baseline, we use the same total
number of training prompts as APT and follow the same rubric-generation
and reward-evaluation procedures. Unless otherwise stated, FLUX.1
\[dev\] is post-trained for $`200`$ optimization steps, while all other
models are post-trained for $`400`$ steps. At inference time, all models
are evaluated at a resolution of $`768\times 768`$ with the following
settings: Lens ($`20`$ steps, CFG $`=5.0`$), SD3.5-M ($`20`$ steps, CFG
$`=4.5`$), FLUX.1 \[dev\] ($`16`$ steps, CFG $`=3.5`$), and
LongCat-Image ($`20`$ steps, CFG $`=4.5`$).

### 3.2 Main Results

In
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
we apply APT to four different base models and compare each APT-trained
model against two counterparts: its original base model and a version
post-trained on a recent *handcrafted* RL training set proposed by
Lens ([Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib6)) and manually curated by human
experts. Importantly, all APT experiments use the same agentic workflow,
without any model-specific prompt sets, reward designs, or
hyperparameter tuning. We draw two main conclusions:

- •
  APT Consistently Outperforms a Carefully Handcrafted RL Training Set
  Across All Four Base Models. The handcrafted RL set is carefully
  curated by human experts to cover a broad range of generation
  scenarios, making it a strong post-training baseline. Nevertheless,
  APT consistently achieves higher average performance across all four
  models. This suggests that manually designing RL training sets may not
  be necessary: human experts may struggle to anticipate all relevant
  failure modes or fully characterize the model-specific output
  distribution, whereas APT can automatically diagnose each model and
  adapt its training data accordingly.
- •
  A Single APT Run Yields Consistent Improvements Across Multiple
  Benchmarks. Without using benchmark-specific training prompts or
  tuning, the same post-trained model improves over its base model
  across most evaluated benchmarks. This demonstrates strong
  benchmark-agnostic generalization, showing that APT does not rely on
  optimization toward any particular benchmark.

### 3.3 Ablation Study

APT Captures Model-Specific Training Distributions. We investigate
whether different T2I models exhibit distinct distributions, and whether
APT can automatically adapt its RL data generation to each model. For
each of the four models, we compare the standard APT setting against RL
using the training data accumulated by APT when post-training another
model. As shown in
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
each row corresponds to a target model being post-trained with RL data
generated for different source models, while the diagonal entry
represents the standard APT setting, where the RL data is generated
adaptively for the same target model. The diagonal setting achieves the
best average performance within every row across all four models. These
results indicate that different T2I models exhibit distinct
distributions, making RL data generated for one model suboptimal for
another. APT addresses this issue by continuously diagnosing the current
model and automatically generating RL data tailored to its evolving
distribution, rather than relying on a fixed training set shared across
models. Note that, for efficiency, we post-train each model for 200
steps in this study.

corresponding capability and leads to less balanced improvements across
benchmarks. This result highlights the importance of automatically
constructing a diverse and comprehensive evaluation set for reliable
diagnosis and adaptive post-training.

Ablation on the Iterative Feedback Loop. We study whether repeatedly
refreshing model feedback is necessary for effective post-training. We
compare APT with a variant that continues generating new training
prompts but does not re-diagnose the updated model after each round,
while keeping the total number of training prompts and RL optimization
steps unchanged. As shown in
Table [4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 3.3 Ablation Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
removing the iterative feedback loop consistently degrades performance,
demonstrating the benefit of continuously adapting the training
distribution to the evolving model.

Ablation on the RL Data Generation Agent. We further ablate the
prompt-sampling strategy of the RL Data Generation Agent. Removing part
of the diagnostic criteria leads to a clear performance drop, while
sampling only from the most difficult capabilities is also inferior to
the full strategy. These results show that effective RL data generation
benefits from both comprehensive diagnostic feedback and a balanced
distribution that prioritizes weak capabilities while retaining moderate
and mastered ones. The results are shown in
Table [4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 3.3 Ablation Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
and the detailed instruction prompts for the two ablation settings are
provided in
Appendix [E.5](#A5.SS5 "E.5 Prompt for the RL Data Generation Agent in the Reduced Diagnostic Criteria Ablation ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation")
and
Appendix [E.6](#A5.SS6 "E.6 Prompt for the RL Data Generation Agent in the Hard-Only Sampling Ablation ‣ Appendix E Prompt ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").

Architecture Generalization to Autoregressive Generation. We further
evaluate APT on an autoregressive image generation model,
Janus-Pro ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), using GRPO ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib24)) for RL post-training. As shown in
Table [5](#S3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 3.3 Ablation Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
APT consistently outperforms both the original base model and the
handcrafted RL post-training baseline across the evaluated benchmarks.
These results demonstrate that APT is not tied to diffusion-based
generators and can generalize effectively to autoregressive generation
architectures, highlighting its architecture-agnostic nature.

Robustness to Different LLM Backbones. We further examine the
sensitivity of APT to the LLM backbone used by the RL Data Generation
Agent. All tested backbones yield substantial gains in average
performance on Lens, suggesting that APT is robust across the evaluated
LLM families and scales. Detailed results are provided in

## 4 Conclusion

We presented APT, a fully automated framework for adaptive post-training
of text-to-image models. By coordinating evaluation set generation,
model diagnosis, and RL data generation, APT adapts the training
distribution to each model’s evolving capabilities. Experiments across
multiple models and benchmarks show higher average performance than
post-training on handcrafted RL data, while transfer studies and
ablations support the value of model-specific training data and
iterative feedback. These findings highlight feedback-driven task
adaptation as a practical direction for automated post-training and a
step toward recursive self-improvement in text-to-image generation.

## Appendix A Related Work

Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation. Post-training has become a
standard paradigm for adapting pre-trained T2I models to downstream
objectives. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts a model to curated
image–text pairs, with performance gains largely determined by data
filtering, recaptioning, and aesthetic curation, but it remains bounded
by the collected corpus and costly human curation. A complementary line
directly optimizes downstream rewards following the policy-gradient view
of reinforcement learning ([Williams, 1992](#bib.bib37); [Schulman et
al., 2017](#bib.bib38)): DDPO ([Black et al., 2024](#bib.bib39))
formulates denoising as a multi-step decision-making problem and
optimizes diffusion models with policy gradients;
Diffusion-DPO ([Wallace et al., 2024](#bib.bib41)) adapts direct
preference optimization ([Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib40)) to
diffusion models, and SPO ([Liang et al., 2024](#bib.bib44)) refines it
with step-aware preference signals; more recently, Flow-GRPO ([Liu et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib23)) and follow-ups ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib42);
[Liu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib43)) extend online policy-gradient training
to flow matching via stochastic sampling, and DiffusionNFT ([Zheng et
al., 2026](#bib.bib22)) performs negative-aware fine-tuning on the
forward process without likelihood estimation.

Agentic Image Generation. Recent work augments image generation and
editing with agentic capabilities such as planning ([Yao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31)), reasoning over implicit user intent ([He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib32)), web and image search for open-world grounding ([Feng
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib33)), and self-feedback for test-time
scaling ([Jiang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib34); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib35)), with emerging systems unifying these abilities in a
single framework ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib36)).

These methods share a common design: *the agent operates at inference
time around a frozen generator*, improving how a fixed model is used
rather than changing the model itself. As a result, intrinsic failure
modes persist once the agentic scaffolding is removed, and every
deployment pays the extra inference cost. APT instead moves the agent
from the inference loop into the *post-training* loop: discover model
weaknesses through evaluation and address them through training. The
gains are absorbed into the model parameters and retained under standard
single-pass inference, and the training distribution is re-derived from
the current model at every round, making APT *model-adaptive* rather
than applying one fixed agentic policy to any generator. The two
directions are thus complementary: prior work makes better use of a
given model, while APT makes the model itself better.

## Appendix B More Ablation Studies

Robustness to Different LLM Backbones in the RL Data Generation Agent.
We investigate how sensitive APT is to the choice of LLM backbone used
by the RL Data Generation Agent. Using Lens as the base image generation
model, we replace the default GPT-5.4 backbone with LLMs from different
families and model scales, while keeping all other components of the
post-training pipeline fixed. As shown in
Table [6](#A2.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix B More Ablation Studies ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation"),
all tested LLM backbones lead to effective post-training and achieve
comparable improvements across the five benchmarks, despite noticeable
differences in their absolute performance. This suggests that the
effectiveness of APT does not depend on a specific LLM family or scale,
and that the RL Data Generation Agent remains robust across diverse
proprietary and open-source backbones.

## Appendix C Detailed Benchmark Results

We evaluate APT on five benchmarks, with the details of each benchmark
described as follows:

- •
  GenEval ([Ghosh et al., 2023](#bib.bib1)) focuses on object-centric
  compositional alignment, with 553 prompts spanning six templated
  tasks: single-object generation, two-object co-occurrence, counting,
  color, spatial relation, and attribute binding. It uses detector- and
  classifier-based verification to assess whether generated images
  satisfy these structured constraints.
- •
  OneIG-EN ([Chang et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) is the English split of
  OneIG-Bench, comprising 1,120 prompts across general objects,
  portraits, anime/stylization, text rendering, and knowledge/reasoning.
  It evaluates generated images with dimension-specific scores for
  subject alignment, text accuracy, reasoning, style, diversity, and
  overall performance.
- •
  GenEval2 ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) extends GenEval with 800
  prompts of increasing compositionality, covering 40 objects, 18
  attributes, 9 relations, and counts from 2 to 7. Each prompt contains
  3 to 10 visual atoms, including objects, attributes, counts, and
  relations, and is evaluated using Soft-TIFA, which decomposes prompts
  into atom-level visual questions and aggregates soft correctness
  scores to measure fine-grained compositional alignment. Soft-TIFA_(AM)
  averages these scores arithmetically within each image to estimate
  atom-level correctness, whereas Soft-TIFA_(GM) uses their geometric
  mean to capture prompt-level correctness by more strongly penalizing
  poorly satisfied atoms. Both variants then average the image-level
  scores arithmetically across the benchmark. We report Soft-TIFA_(GM),
  as the GenEval2 ([Kamath et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) finds that it
  achieves higher AUROC against prompt-level human judgments than
  Soft-TIFA_(AM) across the original, rewritten, and combined prompt
  sets.
- •
  DPG ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)) evaluates dense prompt following
  with 1,065 lengthy prompts describing multiple objects, fine-grained
  attributes, and complex relationships. It decomposes each prompt into
  a dependency-aware question graph and employs an MLLM-based VQA
  evaluator to measure alignment across global, entity, attribute,
  relation, and other semantic dimensions.
- •
  CVTG-2K ([Du et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)) evaluates complex visual text
  generation with multiple text regions, where prompts vary the number
  of regions from 2 to 5 and specify text content, position, length, and
  style attributes such as color, font, and size.

provides the detailed OneIG-EN results corresponding to
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").
We note that RL post-training can substantially reduce generation
diversity, a phenomenon observed for both the Lens ([Chen et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib6)) and Mage-Flow ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib19))
models. Consequently, the Diversity score on OneIG-EN decreases markedly
after RL post-training and may offset improvements in other dimensions,
occasionally resulting in an average score lower than that of the base
model. Nevertheless, the post-trained models consistently exhibit
stronger performance in capability-oriented dimensions such as subject
alignment, text rendering, and reasoning. More importantly, despite the
diversity degradation shared by RL-based approaches, our method w/ APT
generally achieves higher alignment, text, reasoning, and overall scores
than w/ Handcrafted RL Set. These results suggest that APT produces more
effective post-training data and improves the target capabilities more
effectively than handcrafted RL post-training.

## Appendix E Prompt

### E.1 Prompt for Evaluation Prompt Generation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.2 Prompt for Rubric Generation

We adopt the following system prompt to generate rubrics for each
prompt.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### E.3 Prompt for RL Reward Generation

Given a prompt $`p`$ and its corresponding rubrics, we first generate an
image $`x`$ using the current policy model. We then use the same fixed
evaluator $`V`$ (GPT-4.1-mini) as in
Equation [3](#S2.E3 "In 2.2 Diagnosis Agent ‣ 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation")
to score each rubric with the following system prompt. These binary
scores are aggregated into the scalar training reward $`r(x,p)`$ used in
Equation [1](#S2.E1 "In 2 Method ‣ APT: Feedback-Driven Agentic Post-Training for Text-to-Image Generation").

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
````
